recommendations: Konrad Rokicki “I had the pleasure of mentoring Arjun during his internship at Janelia Research Campus. Arjun was tasked with improving our internal RAG-based search engine. He hit the ground running and quickly got up to speed on RAG methods, then set up an effective evaluation pipeline. In fact, he finished the assignment so quickly that we had to scramble to find more work for him. Arjun approaches new challenges in a structured way, and is always eager for feedback and collaboration. He continues to explore new ideas even when the path forward is not obvious. Arjun's methodical problem solving mindset and deep curiosity make him an outstanding engineer, and I would recommend him for any role he pursues in the future.”

activity.title: Last week, Arjun Bakhale and I represented the GreenLight team in San Diego for Biotechnology Innovation Organization 's BIO 2026, our first conference as a company. Getting a clinical trial site activated still takes months and a mountain of manual work. After speaking with sponsors all week, we're more certain than ever that it doesn't have to. A few takeaways: → We had 20+ conversations with biotech sponsors, and the same theme kept surfacing: getting trial sites activated and operational is still slow, manual, and painful. → We sat down with the Director of the FDA's Office of Medical Policy at CDER to talk about where AI fits in clinical operations. → The people closest to site activation know it's broken and are hungry for something better. That's the whole reason GreenLight exists: to take the messy, multi-party work of standing up trial sites worldwide and put it behind a single front door, with a human in the loop. Huge thank you to everyone who made time to talk. We can't wait to initiate our pilots and work together. If we didn't get to connect and you're running multi-site trials, reach out. We'd love to talk! #ClinicalTrials #BIO2026 #LifeSciences

In April, 5 more teams joined LeapYear 2026. We had over 1000+ builders apply and it was our most challenging decision process yet. LeapYear is a first-believer fund for students, dropouts, & grads. We’ve funded 53 teams in the last 2 years. 90%+ were pre-revenue at application and collectively, they have gone on to raise $65+ million in follow-on capital. Congrats to the builders! I build Christmas gifts the same way I validate startup ideas. Socks and candles are nice, but they don't change anyone's life. My gift to my dad this year does. For the past few years, my dad has poured himself into perfecting his home garden. This year, he maxed it out. So he started helping friends and selling spare plants. The problem? He knew his expertise was valuable. He just didn't know how to scale it. That's why I built Raj's Garden ( rajsgarden.shop ) for him this Christmas. The app does two things: → Marketplace for his surplus plants → Booking system for 1-on-1 gardening consultations I built it in just 2 weeks between other projects—proof that you don't need months to ship something valuable. The Stack? Next.js frontend, Express.js backend, Supabase for database and auth. Could I have bought him a nice candle instead? Sure. But this gift gave him something more valuable: the freedom to scale his passion on his own terms. Check it out at rajsgarden.shop ! And if you know anyone looking for gardening advice or quality plants, send them his way. 🌱 The best business ideas aren't always at pitch competitions or hackathons. Sometimes they're sitting right across the dinner table.

How do you 𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀? The answer is… 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀! During my 8-week internship at Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) , I've been: - 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗥𝗔𝗚 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Developing a system using language models to streamline and enhance the assessment of Retrieval-Augmented Generation LLMs, improving efficiency and accuracy. - 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝟯𝟬𝟬%: Building Slack integrations that significantly increased user interaction and productivity within our team's workflow. - 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗗𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀: Constructing containerized applications that run seamlessly across different CPU architectures, improving deployment flexibility and compatibility. - Knee-deep in GitHub commits Huge thanks to my mentor Konrad Rokicki for his invaluable guidance. Also, I am grateful to Erik Snapp and John Chapin, Ph.D. for opening the door to this incredible opportunity. “The answer is always more LLMs”

We won at SpaceXAI ’s Grokathon this past weekend! We took 2nd place by building Signal: an app that indexes your X followers, clusters them, and runs A/B testing with a human behavior engine for your next X post. Our product helps you understand your followers, and figure out how to maximize engagement. Shout out my cracked teammates Aditya Bilawar , Sam Chen , and Jeffrey Zhou for making this possible. Check it out at use-signal.com

I can tell you exactly why Rounds will be a unicorn company And it has nothing to do with AI In fact this concept is something my parents challenge me on often too The biggest challenge a founder faces when hiring is getting attention from the right (often employed) candidates And no AI tool can convince a candidate to take the first interview So we’re focused on building a network of humans that can intro you to the right candidate, 0 AI So to my parents, yes I am not using my PhD in AI. 😅 Not because I can’t, but because the problem I’m trying to solve doesn’t need it

This has been a long time coming. Excited to announce that Kenny Morales is joining the Slashy team as our founding engineer. In less than a month, Kenny has already shipped: > A full iPad app > A complete reskin of our iOS app (now the best-looking mobile email client) > An entirely new landing page from scratch > ~25 PRs a day I remember after day 1 of his work trial at Slashy, Kenny asked me. “Why do people flex shipping 10 PRs in a day that feels so little”. That’s how I knew we had to have him. He’s the unicorn who has taste, and intensity. Can’t wait to build the future of email with Kenny :)

I’m taking a year-long leave of absence from Raikes School to join Slashy as its founding engineer. For the past few years, I’ve bounced between FindU, mkrs, community events, and a lot of random software. Each one taught me something different, but most of my experience has been starting things and figuring them out as I go. To be honest, I didn’t grow up knowing opportunities like this existed. The people who took me seriously and gave me a chance changed the direction of my life. Long term, I want to give other people that same kind of chance and show people who grow up like I did that they can do things like this too. Slashy gives me the chance to focus on one company, take real responsibility, and learn from people I respect. I still have a lot to learn if I want to create those chances for more people. I plan to be back at Raikes in Fall 2027. When I return, I hope I can bring what I’ve learned back to the community that gave me so much. I’m only able to take this opportunity because so many people in Nebraska gave me chances first. It would literally be impossible to describe the impact every person I’ve interacted with here has had on me. I wish I could message each of you individually. If we’ve crossed paths, thank you fr. And thank you to Harsha Gaddipati and Dhruv Roongta for taking a chance on me.

99% of founders quit before winning. because often, making progress doesn’t feel like it at all... When you’re trying to get better at something it’s super easy to feel de-motivated when you don’t immediately see improvement But that exact misery is what makes for progress. What’s worked for me recently is “trusting growth blindly” Which is caring more about effort than outcomes, and trusting it will pay off.
